idiom_name: typed reducer over an immutable discriminated union
implementation_notes: TypeScript does not change the runtime story from JavaScript - the interesting gain is static, not dynamic. TypeScript can make the transactional cell's discipline checkable: if the shared state is typed as `readonly` and every transition is a pure function `(state: State, action: Action) => State`, then a transaction body cannot mutate anything, which is exactly the precondition STM requires (all work in a transaction is speculative). That makes a hand-written STM-shaped helper safe to ship across a codebase in a way it is not in JavaScript, and it makes the reducer form a genuine compile-time-enforced replacement rather than a convention. At runtime the same choice applies as in JavaScript: one-threaded by default, so use the reducer; if state is genuinely shared across workers or Node's cluster worker_threads, use Atomics over a SharedArrayBuffer and a version-tagged CAS loop, and model the cell as a branded type so the atomic surface is the only thing the shared code can touch.
alternative: pure reducer over a readonly State union (compile-time enforced purity); Atomics.compareExchange over a SharedArrayBuffer for genuine cross-worker sharing
pitfalls: Typing state as a mutable shape (no readonly) so `readonly` purity is a suggestion and the reducer mutates in place.
Casting away readonly with `as` inside a transition, which reintroduces the mutation the type system was protecting.
Optional fields silently becoming undefined mid-transition: `balances[a.to] ?? 0` hides a missing account instead of failing.
Forgetting that `readonly` is shallow - a nested mutable array in the state defeats the snapshot just as it defeats copy-on-write.
Assuming the type system makes a CAS loop safe: it cannot prove the loop re-reads every location it depends on before recomputing.
